name: Boundary extension
statement: People remember a photographed scene as showing more of the world than it did, and the error runs the other way for wide views of distant space.
meaning: The claim is that memory for a view is not a copy of the view. Shown a close-up photograph and asked to draw it, people draw the cropped objects whole and add ground, wall and sky that the camera never captured. Shown the identical photograph a second time, they rate it as a closer view than the one they saw. Intraub's account is that scene perception runs past the edges of the input, and that the extrapolated surround is later remembered as having been seen. The standard recognition measure is a five-point rating scale running from much closer-up through the same to much farther-away, set out that way in Gagnier and Intraub's Scholarpedia article. Two things follow that the short version of the claim leaves out. The direction is not fixed. Views of a single close object extend in memory, and wide views of a room or a landscape contract, with a crossover point in between. The error also shows up when there is almost nothing to remember, including while a person copies a photograph that is still in front of them.

origin.where: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
origin.note: The paper named the effect and reported two experiments, a memory drawing task and a boundary rating task. Its full text is closed at APA. Its abstract was read at PubMed and Europe PMC, and gives 37 undergraduates in the drawing experiment and 85 in the boundary recognition experiment.

evidence: Intraub and Richardson's abstract reports 37 undergraduates who viewed 20 pictures for 15 seconds each. It states that 95% of their drawings included information that had not been physically present but would have lain just outside the camera's field of view. A second experiment had 85 undergraduates rate targets and distractors on a boundary-placement scale, and they rated the target pictures as closer up than before. The full article is closed at APA, so the rest of the 1989 work is described here from Gagnier and Intraub's Scholarpedia article, which Intraub curates. Their Figure 1 shows a close-up and a wide-angle photograph of the same scene beside drawings made from memory of each, and in both cases the drawings run past all four edges of the photograph. Intraub and Bodamer then tested whether the error is an artefact of not knowing what is coming. Eighty-one subjects viewed 12 photographs of simple scenes for 15 seconds each under one of three instructions: remember the picture in detail, the same plus a warning about the tests to come, or the same plus a demonstration of boundary extension and an instruction to guard against it. A drawing task and a boundary recognition test followed. Warning sometimes reduced the distortion and never removed it. McDunn, Siddiqui and Brown stripped the scenes of meaning, building close-angle and wide-angle displays from irregular geometric shapes that independent raters found unrecognisable, on random-dot or blank backgrounds. Boundary extension appeared in every condition, which puts object recognition and scene schemas outside the list of things it requires. Hafri, Wadhwa and Bonner ran seven experiments with 1,100 adults recruited, using tilt shift, a photographic trick that makes a real place look like a scale model by cutting apparent viewing distance while leaving the rest of the image alone. Their first experiment recruited 100 and analysed 93 after preregistered exclusions. Viewers called the probe the closer view on 69.3% of fake-miniaturised trials against 51.7% of original trials, odds ratio 2.32, 95% interval 1.88 to 2.86. The effect ran the same way for 73 of the 93 people and for 30 of the 32 scenes, and it held for a second, unrelated distance manipulation. Pullinen, Mononen, Simola and Henriksson took the effect out of the picture frame. Sixty people wearing a virtual reality headset looked freely around each of 20 rooms, then returned and walked to the spot they thought they had viewed from. They stopped too far back, so that their field of view was wider than the original, for close-up views, t = 4.29, p < 0.001, and across all conditions, t = 3.26, p = 0.001. For the far views the error did not differ from zero, t = 1.44, p = 0.156. Nothing in that display had a visible border, so borders are not what the effect needs.

examples.tag: The photograph that lost its edges
examples.text: Asked to draw a snapshot of a cat on a doorstep, someone draws the whole step, a stretch of path and a strip of sky the camera never held. Shown the original again, he rates it as a closer view than the one he was given.

examples.tag: The hall that shrinks in memory
examples.text: A wide shot of an empty hall runs the other way. Asked to recall it, people picture less of the hall than the picture showed, which is why the error is not the mind simply adding more of everything it sees.

examples.tag: The copy made with the picture still there
examples.text: Copying a photograph that has not been taken away, a person still adds ground beyond the frame. Nothing has been forgotten, so the extra cannot be the edges slipping quietly out of memory.

replication.headline: Boundary extension repeats across laboratories, response measures and virtual reality, but only for close views: across 1,000 photographs judged by 2,000 people, object-centred images extended 93.2% of the time while wide scene images split evenly between extension and contraction.
replication.detail: Bainbridge and Baker assembled 500 object-oriented images from Google Open Images and 500 scene-oriented images from the Scene Understanding Database, and ran two rapid recognition experiments of 1,000 participants each, 200 judgments per image. On the object-oriented set, the kind used in most earlier work, 93.2% of images produced extension and 6.8% contraction, chi-squared = 746.5. On the scene-oriented set, 49.0% extended and 49.8% contracted, chi-squared = 0.06, p = 0.800. Whether a given image extends or contracts is a property of the image rather than noise. With two response options the split-half reliability was 0.80 for the object set and 0.79 for the scene set; with three options it was 0.76 and 0.71. The two experiments correlated at rho = 0.84. Direction tracked composition. Boundary transformation correlated with the number of objects at rho = 0.58, with rated distance to the main object at rho = 0.76, and negatively with average object area at rho = -0.49. The 200 most extending images held a mean of 2.4 objects against 15.4 for the 200 most contracting. Reanalysing 728 drawings that 24 people made while looking at the photograph, 63.3% of the 60 scenes contracted and 35.0% extended, chi-squared = 9.64, p = 0.002, so the distortion survives with the stimulus in view. Park, Josephs and Konkle built virtual rooms and sampled views along a continuous approach, from object close-up to wide indoor view, testing 377 participants. Close views extended, far views contracted, and the crossover was orderly, rho = 0.66 between position and distortion. It fell at position 12.5 of the continuum, bootstrap 95% interval 11.2 to 16.2, and tracked which view people judged best-looking rather than which view was within arm's reach. They state that none of their studies was preregistered. Hall and Geng showed the direction can be pushed by attention alone. Thirty-six people studied 15 scenes while searching for a target and 36 others simply memorised them. Search drawings contracted on 62.29% of occasions and extended on 30.73%, chi-squared(1, N = 283) = 28.0, p < 0.001, while memorise drawings split 44.67% against 47.95%, chi-squared(1, N = 232) = 0.04, p > 0.5. Compared scene by scene across the 15 images the difference held, Z = 2.32, p = 0.020. Intraub replied in Current Biology that Bainbridge and Baker's conclusions outrun their data, and that neither the universality they attack nor the narrow recycled stimulus set they blame describes the field fairly. Bainbridge and Baker's reply sets out her two-mechanism position, scene construction producing extension alone and normalisation producing errors in both directions, and answers that it assumes what is in question. Gandolfo, Nagele and Peelen then put the reversal itself in question. Across four experiments with 125 adults they found that boundary extension depends on depth of field, and that photographs with naturalistic depth of field gave larger extension than photographs with unnaturalistic depth of field even when distant views were shown. Hubbard's review reports that they also reanalysed Bainbridge and Baker's data and found extension much more common than contraction among photographs whose depth of field resembles human vision. That reanalysis figure is taken from the review rather than from their own paper.

study.cite: Bainbridge, W. A., & Baker, C. I. (2020). Boundaries extend and contract in scene memory depending on image properties. Current Biology, 30(3), 537-543.e3.

limits: No meta-analysis of boundary extension was located. The search ran on 21 September 2026 across Crossref, OpenAlex, PubMed, Europe PMC, Unpaywall and the open web. It also ran across the whole text of Hubbard's 2024 review, 42 pages in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review, which names none. Several papers here were reached only in part. Intraub and Richardson's 1989 article is closed at APA, and this entry reports the two sample sizes and the 95% figure its abstract carries and nothing further. Intraub's 2020 correspondence and Bainbridge and Baker's reply are listed as open by OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall. Every copy those indexes name sits on cell.com, which answered with a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall on 21 September 2026, as did ScienceDirect. Neither correspondence was read, and the abstracts at Europe PMC are all this entry rests on for them. Multhaup, Munger, Yoo, Hu and Faust report in Visual Cognition that boundary extension replicates outside Western samples. Their publisher answers with a Cloudflare challenge too, so only their abstract is quoted: 36 adults recruited near Busan and Seoul, 36 near Beijing, and 36 near Charlotte, North Carolina as a comparison group for each, with significant boundary extension in both East Asian groups and no difference across cultural groups. McDunn, Siddiqui and Brown's paper is closed at Springer, and the Columbus State repository record for it holds no file, so it is described from its Europe PMC abstract. Gandolfo, Nagele and Peelen's four experiments are described from their PubMed and Europe PMC abstract and from Hubbard's review. Hubbard's review, Bainbridge and Baker's report, Hafri and colleagues' paper, Park and colleagues' paper, Hall and Geng's paper and Pullinen and colleagues' paper were read in full. Within the effect itself, the size depends on the retention interval, the response measure and how many pictures a person has to hold. Gagnier and Intraub note that the error can disappear with sets larger than about 24 pictures, where people lose track of the boundaries and err in both directions at random. Pullinen and colleagues' virtual reality task explained little of the variance, marginal R-squared 0.038 against conditional 0.14, most of it individual differences between participants.
misreadings: The most common retelling now inverts the finding it is trying to report. Boundary extension is said to reverse for close-up views, when close-up views are the case that extends and wide views of distant space are the case that contracts. Every result here points the same way, including the one that started the argument: on Bainbridge and Baker's object-centred close-ups, 93.2% of images extended. Bainbridge and Baker are also read as having shown the effect is not real. Their claim is about scope, that extension is one of two equally common distortions rather than a universal property of scene memory, and they proposed removing it from textbooks on that ground, not on the ground that it does not happen. Contraction is then read as ordinary forgetting of the edges. It appeared in 63.3% of drawings made by people looking at the photograph while they drew, which is not a memory failure. The effect is also grouped with the implanted memories of the false-memory literature, and the two are not the same kind of error. Boundary extension needs no suggestion, no misinformation and no delay. Gagnier and Intraub report it for presentations as short as 250 milliseconds, for breaks in the input of 42 milliseconds, and in infants as young as three months, and Pullinen and colleagues found it in a headset with no picture frame anywhere in the display. Knowing about it does not fix it. Intraub and Bodamer gave one group a demonstration of the phenomenon and told them to guard against it, and the distortion shrank without going away.

The paper that named the effect. Metadata verified at Crossref and OpenAlex. The full text is closed at APA and was not read; the abstract was read at PubMed, PMID 2522508, and at Europe PMC, and supplies the two sample sizes and the 95% figure quoted here.

Curated by Intraub, and secondary with respect to her own 1989 paper.
